newsitem.title: USA: Election again highlights Miami race gap.
newsitem.headline: Election again highlights Miami race gap.

text.p: Miami voters were set to head to the polls this week for the second local election in less than two months to pit the city's Latin-American community against its African-Americans.

In the runoff vote set for Thursday, Humberto Hernandez, a 34-year-old Cuban-American lawyer, was to vie with 35-year-old Rev. Richard Dunn, who is an African-American, for the city commission seat left open by the departure of Miller Dawkins.

Dawkins, who held a commission seat widely considered the "black" one, pleaded guilty to bribery Oct. 9 in the midst of a major City Hall scandal and a $68 million, or 20 percent, budget deficit that has prompted a petition drive seeking the dissolution of Miami and its absorption into Dade County.
The Dunn-Hernandez race appeared close. Hernandez edged Dunn in the Nov. 5 eight-candidate primary by 29,991 to 28,268 votes.
But most of the candidates in the runoff were Latin- American, including Margarita Ruiz, who finished third with 12 percent, and has endorsed Hernandez and attacked Dunn.

Fifty-five percent of all votes in the primary were cast for Hispanic candidates, a bad omen for hopes within the African-American community of retaining a city commission seat held by blacks since 1965. Dunn was backed by only about 15 percent of Hispanics.
Forty-nine percent of the 133,192 registered voters in Miami are Hispanic, while just 26 percent are black. And Miami's voters tend to vote along ethnic lines.

That ethnic loyalty outweighs even party loyalty in the Miami area was sharply displayed Oct. 1, when 92 percent of Dade County's Hispanic voters, most of them traditionally Republican Cuban-Americans who crossed party lines, voted to elect Alex Penelas, a 34-year-old Cuban-American Democrat, as the first executive mayor of Dade County.
And 95 percent of the city's traditionally Democratic black voters backed Republican Arthur Teele. Teele, an African-American, lost to Penelas by 60 to 40 percent.
That campaign was marked by acrimonious racial attacks by supporters of the two men, particularly on radio stations.

One Spanish-language station asked Cubans to address "a problem with race" in voting. And a black station alluded to a "master plan by Cubans" to take over Dade County and warned that Spanish might become the region's official language.

"There is a resentment on the part of the black community for the emergence of the power of the Cuban community, both political, economic and social," said Ric Katz, a Miami political strategist who is not involved in the Dunn-Hernandez race.

"There has always been a desire on the part of the black community to have a representative on the city commission," he said. "This is a large population in Dade County, in the city of Miami, that sees the loss of that seat as a loss of social recognition and the loss of access to city hall."
Katz added, "On the part of the Hispanic community, there's a feeling that it's a seat, and it doesn't have a label on it, and anyone should be entitled to seek it."

The Dunn-Hernandez race quickly shaped itself along racial lines. Dunn has said Hernandez cannot represent African- Americans. "He cannot speak ever for the community, because he doesn't know what it's like to be black," Dunn told the Miami Herald. "If I wanted to speak for Cubans, I couldn't. I can empathize. But I don't know what it's like to be Cuban."
And while Cuban-American leaders including Miami Mayor Joe Carrollo have backed Dunn's candidacy, others have aligned themselves behind Hernandez.
On Wednesday Hernandez appeared on a Spanish-language radio station and said black radio was saying Cubans were "taking over" the city. Dunn denied the contention.
